newsitem.title: FRANCE: French strike trims news output in tax protest.
newsitem.headline: French strike trims news output in tax protest.

text.p: A one-day journalists' strike pared French public broadcasters and news agencies to minimum service on Tuesday in a protest at government plans to scrap their profession's 62-year-old tax break.

The stoppage fired a warning shot across the centre-right government's bows as civil servants, teachers, rail and power workers prepared for a 24-hour strike on Thursday against cutbacks and record unemployment.
State-owned television channels ran short news bulletins, but private 24-hour news broadcaster LCI offered a full service. Music dominated the France-Info radio news channel.

The strike restricted French-language services from the news agencies Agence France-Presse (AFP), Associated Press and Reuters. An editor at AFP said text, graphics and picture services were disrupted.

Staff at newspaper Le Monde voted not to join the strike but many other newspapers, especially regional ones, will not appear on Wednesday in the protest over plans to scrap a 30 percent income tax deduction for professional expenses which journalists say is effectively part of their salary.

Prime Minister Alain Juppe has refused to go back on a pledge to scrap tax breaks for some 100 professions including journalism. But he asked Finance Minister Jean Arthuis to ensure the application of the measure did not put any groups at a disadvantage.

An official in the premier's office said this especially concerned unmarried journalists earning the profession's average wage of 12,000 francs ($2,320) a month. "As Juppe said, everyone must gain from tax reform," the official said.
The government plans to phase out the journalists' deduction over five years along with dozens of other breaks for various professions as part of a reform that will cut income tax for most taxpayers.

"The government plan, if it is carried out with its current brutality, will penalise the wages of most journalists to the tune of a month's wage," wrote Serge July, former editor of the left-leaning daily Liberation.
"The attitude of the executive highlights its hostility towards journalists," he added, a reference to government plans to crack down on media coverage of corruption probes.
In the most extreme case, a single journalist earning 15,000 francs ($2,900) a month will end up paying 60 percent more tax after the reform than before it, government figures show.
Unions representing nearly 30,000 journalists called a demonstration outside parliament as the National Assembly began debating the 1997 budget bill.

With more than three million people out of work and tens of thousands more set to lose their jobs through public spending cuts, Thursday's strike should show if the will is there for the kind of showdown which crippled the country late last year.
All the main civil service unions have joined in the strike call, including local and national administrations and hospital staff.
Unions representing teachers, railway, gas and electricity workers have all joined the stoppage and private doctors who are fighting health spending controls are also to stop work.
